rv.q: That the characters also live in a world of ideas gives the play its intellectual heft and complex texture, both light and profound.
'Infinite Life,' Annie Baker's tender and compassionate but staunchly unsentimental new play about people living with chronic pain and disease.
Among our playwrights, only Baker can illuminate such transient episodes with such feeling and insight. I don't know how she does it.

Baker dissects a seemingly mundane situation with little theatricality but with such unexpected humor and heartbreaking reality that we recognize ourselves in its quiet, shatteringly relatable moments.
Pain may be trapped in the sufferer's body, but great acting in such primal, honest drama can soothe a collective hurt.
Baker deserves much thanks for that.

Under James Macdonald's superb direction, we watch five women and one man read, sleep, talk and sip water or juice on the patio of a wellness clinic in Northern California trying to deal with their chronic pain.
If 'Infinite Life' doesn't quite knit together into a fully satisfying whole, it's always worthwhile to see what's currently on the playwright's mind.
'Infinite Life' has much to say about the ideas it explores, and it does so with laser-sharp exactitude.
Baker isolates the simple act of existing as (or in) a body and shows us how it's not so simple.
Baker is not just demonstrating that misery loves company but positing that misery also leads to real human connection.
Those rewards felt fewer this time around.
The ensemble is composed of a gallery of estimable theatrical pros, but they have so little to work with that even such normally standout performers as Burke and Nielsen barely make an impression.
It is the kind of play that people will be talking about for a long, long time.
There is incremental healing among the six as they share stories about their lives and their pain, as they read, and color, and sip.
This maneuver shows Baker's determination to avoid melodrama—there is no rupture of friendship, death of a patient, or bite-sized nuggets of wisdom.
Abnegation is seldom a path to compelling drama, and the issues raised in 'Infinite Life' seldom probe very far beneath the surface level.
